title: Inject real secret values only at the outbound tool boundary, leaving placeholders in agent-visible state.
description:
The Slack client / tool layer swaps a placeholder for the real token only at the moment of the outbound API call; nothing the agent can read or echo holds the live value. Mirrors the peer runtime's MITM credential proxy (placeholder in, real value swapped at egress) adapted to CCSC's in-process model.

Acceptance: agent-visible state and tool inputs contain only placeholders; the real token is resolved at the outbound boundary and never returned in a tool result; tests assert no live token appears in agent-readable surfaces.

Provenance: the peer-runtime audit pattern catalog distilled in 000-docs/ADR-002-architecture-patterns-from-peer-runtime-audit.md, and the private engagement decision record AT-DECR 013 (contributing-clanker/000-docs/013-AT-DECR). No peer brand is named in this repo by design.
notes:
CONFLICT REVIEW (2026-06-03): The placeholder-swap at the outbound boundary is a NEW injection seam (ADR-002 Consequences). It must carry its own test: (a) no live token appears in any agent-readable surface, AND (b) the swap point itself cannot be coerced into emitting the real value to the wrong destination.
PREMISE FINDING (2026-06-03, before claiming): ADR-002 §1 says 'the Claude process reads raw .env tokens in-process' — but CCSC's actual architecture is an MCP-stdio split (ARCHITECTURE.md L33: Claude Code SPAWNS server.ts as a child stdio subprocess). The bot/app tokens live ONLY in the bridge (child) process and flow ONLY into Slack-bound sinks: new WebClient(botToken), new SocketModeClient({appToken}), and one Authorization: Bearer header in download_attachment (server.ts:1426). They are NEVER placed in a tool result or MCP notification — verified by grepping every botToken/appToken reference. So the agent (parent process) cannot read the token at all. CONCLUSION: the peer's placeholder-swap injection (placeholders in agent-visible state, swap at boundary) is REDUNDANT in CCSC — the goal ('agent never holds the raw token; real value only at the outbound boundary') is already met structurally by the process split. RE-SCOPE: .2's deliverable becomes (a) a runtime defense-in-depth inbound value-guard symmetric to .3 — scrub/block any declared-secret value from a tool result before it returns to the agent, derived from the same SECRET_DECLARATIONS set — and (b) a THREAT-MODEL/ADR note documenting that CCSC achieves placeholder-swap's guarantee architecturally, so no in-process placeholder layer is added. This honors .2's stated acceptance ('real token never returned in a tool result; tests assert no live token in agent-readable surfaces') without building a redundant placeholder mechanism. Engineer's call per autonomy; recorded for the readable trail.

title: Make outbound sends idempotent so redelivery never double-posts.
description:
Give each obligation a stable idempotency key so a retry after an ambiguous failure (send succeeded but the ack was lost) does not post the reply twice. Mirrors the peer runtime's idempotent final-delivery.

Acceptance: a send carries a deterministic idempotency key derived from the obligation; a replayed send with the same key is a no-op (dedup on key, or chat.update of the prior message); tests assert at-most-once visible delivery under simulated ack loss.

title: Add a leased delivery poller that retries and dead-letters non-retryable Slack errors.
description:
A poller claims pending outbox obligations under a lease (reusing 1-A's fencing), sends, and on failure classifies the Slack error: retryable (rate_limit, transient 5xx, network) → backoff and retry; non-retryable (channel_not_found, not_in_channel, invalid_auth) → dead-letter with the error recorded. Replaces today's stderr-and-swallow.

Acceptance: retryable errors are retried with backoff up to a cap; non-retryable errors move the obligation to dead-letter without infinite retry; the poller honors a lease so two processes never double-send; tests cover both error classes and lease contention.

Provenance: the peer-runtime audit pattern catalog distilled in 000-docs/ADR-002-architecture-patterns-from-peer-runtime-audit.md, and the private engagement decision record AT-DECR 013 (contributing-clanker/000-docs/013-AT-DECR). No peer brand is named in this repo by design.

title: Record a durable delivery obligation when a turn reaches a terminal state.
description:
When a turn goes terminal, write a durable "reply owed" obligation (channel, thread, payload ref, attempt count, state) before attempting the Slack send — a transactional outbox. The send is then a consumer of the obligation, not a fire-and-forget side effect.

Acceptance: reaching terminal state persists an outbox obligation atomically with the turn's terminal marker; a crash after terminal-but-before-send leaves a pending obligation the poller can later honor; tests assert the obligation is written on terminal transition.

title: Add a per-turn fencing lease and heartbeat to the session supervisor.
description:

title: Make Slack sessions crash-safe and replies loss-proof.
description:
Harden CCSC's session runtime against process crashes and dropped replies, borrowing the peer runtime's durability primitives (lease-fenced durable execution, transactional-outbox reliable delivery, crash recovery).

Today: supervisor crash recovery is reload-only with no fencing — two processes can both believe they own a turn — and a failed chat.postMessage is logged to stderr and swallowed (audit-journal-architecture.md invariant 1: the projection may never block tool execution), so a terminal turn can produce no Slack reply with no retry. The peer runtime solves both with a worker lease + per-thread advisory lock and a durable agent_final_delivery_outbox; we adopt the patterns, not the code.

Split into two sub-epics: 1-A (lease-fenced durable execution + recovery) and 1-B (reliable delivery outbox). 1-B depends on 1-A's lease/state model.

title: 31-B.7: Test — round-trip publish → re-read returns equivalent manifest

title: 31-B.3: Replace semantics — pins.list → remove prior → post → pins.add
description: Find any existing pinned manifest from this bot_id. pins.remove it. Post new manifest message. pins.add. Atomic-ish (no two manifests pinned at once, worst case transient gap).
close_reason: Replace semantics shipped in PR #119 (paired with ccsc-0qk.1). Before posting, publish_manifest calls pins.list(channel) and filters to messages whose bot_id/user matches ours AND whose text contains the magic header, then pins.remove each prior manifest. Best-effort: pins.list and individual pins.remove failures are logged and skipped so a flaky Slack call never blocks the publish — worst case an extra pin survives until the next publish sweeps it up. Journal event carries replaced-count so operators can verify the sweep ran.

title: 31-B.4: In-memory rate limiter — 1 publish per channel per hour
description: Map<channelId, lastPublishAt>. Reject second publish within 1h with clear error. Prevents pinning spam. Not persisted — restart resets.
close_reason: 1-publish/channel/hour rate limiter shipped in PR #121. PUBLISH_RATE_LIMIT_MS = 3_600_000 ms in manifest.ts + createPublishRateLimiter factory with injected time source, 256-entry soft-LRU, and checkAndRecord() that reserves the slot BEFORE the caller publishes (non-rollback — a retry-on-failure limiter would be trivially bypassable). Wired into server.ts publish_manifest handler between size cap and replace sweep; rejection journals gate.outbound.deny. Rejection error carries channel + elapsed minutes + remaining minutes so operators know when they can retry. 10 tests pin the contract: constant, first-publish, second-within-window, boundary exclusive at windowMs, post-window refresh, channel isolation, clear, soft-LRU eviction, default window, remaining-time format. 574/574 tests pass, typecheck clean.

title: 31-B.2: Publish-size cap — 8KB (stricter than read)

close_reason: 8 KB publish-side size cap shipped in PR #120. close_reason: Deferred to v0.7.x (superseded by ccsc-4nm). Design rationale: MCP's permission-relay protocol has no tool-completion notification — we send permissions/response allow, Claude executes in its own process, no outcome surfaces back through the MCP channel. Shipping a synthesized outcome via proxy heuristics (timer-based 'assumed done', next-action correlation) would produce receipts LESS trustworthy than the authoritative hash-chained journal they project. The pre-exec receipt (Epic 30-B.2 / PR #106) is the complete projection surface; outcome data lives in audit.log and is accessible via --verify-audit-log. Follow-up bead ccsc-4nm will wire the post-exec edit when one of these lands: (a) MCP spec adds a tool-completion notification; (b) we relocate tool execution into server.ts proper to observe outcomes directly; (c) operator-facing need demonstrably requires inventing a lossy status. title: 30-A.3: Trusted-anchor timestamp (ISO-8601 UTC + monotonic counter)

The design-doc ts/seq pair matches the bead's intent. Separately, the TRUSTED_ANCHOR concept from audit-journal-architecture.md §76-85 (anchor-in-first-event-body) is NOT yet enforced — writer generates an anchor as prevHash but doesn't write it into the event body. If that's the missing piece, file a new bead; otherwise this one can close.

title: Wire SOPS+age boot-time loading of audit-signing key into server.ts
description:

Concrete scope:
- At server boot, before JournalWriter.open(): spawn sops -d ~/.claude/channels/slack/audit.key.sops.yaml via child_process; pipe stdout to parseKeyPairYaml; pass the resulting Ed25519KeyPair into JournalWriter.open({ signingKey, policyDigest }).
- policyDigest: compute via policyDigest(rules) from policy.ts at every policy load (boot + hot-reload). Update writer.setPolicyDigest(...) on reload.
- Decrypted YAML is held in memory only — NEVER written to /dev/shm or any disk path. (Earlier draft of key-management.md mentioned /dev/shm; we don't need it since the SOPS pipe is in-memory.)
- --no-audit-signing CLI flag emergency valve per 000-docs/key-management.md (refuses to load key, writer falls back to v1).
- Boot fails loud (exit code 2) if SOPS file present but malformed (per parseKeyPairYaml throws). Boot succeeds with v1 mode if SOPS file absent AND --no-audit-signing is set.
- 90-day rotation reminder: a stderr log line if createdAt is older than 90 days. NOT a hard failure — operators may choose to defer.

Acceptance:
- Fresh boot with valid SOPS file → JournalWriter emits v2 signed events
- Boot with malformed SOPS file → process.exit(2) with clear message
- Boot with no SOPS file + --no-audit-signing → v1 mode (existing behavior preserved)

title: Refactor 4 complexity outliers + tighten crap-score threshold to 30
description:
## Context

`scripts/crap-score.ts` (shipped in PR #135 / ccsc-gh0) measures TS-aware cyclomatic complexity across the six production source files. CI currently gates at `--threshold 85` — a regression-only gate tuned to the current ceiling. The Wall 5 ideal per the `/audit-tests` skill is **30**. Four functions today sit above that ideal and block tightening:

| # | File:line | Function | Complexity | Gap to 30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `lib.ts:1113` | `gate()` | 32 | +2 |
| 2 | `server.ts:2066` | `handleMessage` | 35 | +5 |
| 3 | `server.ts:1777` | `<anon>` — `socket.on('interactive', ...)` handler | 39 | +9 |
| 4 | `server.ts:850` | `<anon>` — `mcp.setRequestHandler(CallToolRequestSchema, ...)` | 84 | +54 |

`lib.ts` outliers: 1 function. `server.ts` outliers: 3 functions (the two anons sit at the Socket Mode → MCP boundary; `handleMessage` is the inbound event dispatcher).

`policy.ts`, `manifest.ts`, `journal.ts`, `supervisor.ts` — all functions are already ≤ 15 complexity. No action needed there.

## Why this matters

Threshold 85 works as a regression gate but lets new functions land at very high complexity without challenge. Tightening to 30 forces every future PR to decompose up-front instead of relying on future refactor passes. It also matches the skill's rubric, so our CRAP gate is directly comparable to other repos using the same audit methodology.

## Per-function decomposition strategy

### 1. `gate()` at `lib.ts:1113` (32 → target ≤ 30)

Structure today (5 inline numbered blocks in the comment):
1. Bot message handling — self-echo + per-channel opt-in + PERMISSION_REPLY_RE
2. Drop non-message subtypes
3. No user_id → drop
4. DM handling — allowlist check, dmPolicy branch, pairing code lookup, pending-cap check, new code generation
5. Channel handling — opt-in + allowFrom + requireMention

**Proposed extractions (all pure, all testable in isolation):**
- `handleBotEvent(ev, opts): GateResult | null` — returns a `drop` result when the event is a self-echo / not-opted-in / permission-reply-shaped, returns `null` when the bot event should fall through to normal channel-policy checks. Removes branch depth ~8 from `gate()`.
- `handleDmEvent(ev, opts): GateResult` — extract the entire `channel_type === 'im'` block including pairing-code issuance. Removes branch depth ~9.

After extraction `gate()` becomes a short top-level router (~10 complexity):

```ts
if (ev.bot_id) { const r = handleBotEvent(ev, opts); if (r) return r }
if (ev.subtype && ev.subtype !== 'file_share') return { action: 'drop' }
if (!ev.user) return { action: 'drop' }
if (ev.channel_type === 'im') return handleDmEvent(ev, opts)
return handleChannelEvent(ev, opts)
```

**Risk: HIGH.** `gate()` is the primary inbound security boundary. Coverage: `server.test.ts` has 30+ tests around `gate()`; `features/steps/gate.ts` runs all 10 scenarios from `inbound_gate.feature` against it. Refactor must keep both suites green bit-for-bit, including Stryker survivors killed in ccsc-y4e. Sub-agent review before merge is strongly advised.

### 2. `handleMessage` at `server.ts:2066` (35 → target ≤ 30)

Today: a single `switch(result.action)` on gate's return, with `drop` / `pair` / `deliver` branches. The `deliver` branch is ~60 lines and does: thread-tracking, journal write, file download, text rewrite, MCP notification. That's the bulk of the complexity.

**Proposed extraction:**
- `deliverEvent(ev, access, ...): Promise<void>` — move the entire `case 'deliver':` body into its own async function. `handleMessage` collapses to a thin dispatcher over the three action kinds.

**Risk: MEDIUM.** Pure refactor; no behavior change. Coverage is integration-shaped through the socket.on('message') callbacks which are harder to exercise in unit tests, but existing tests on gate + libDeliveredThreadKey + mcp.notification flows still hold.

### 3. `socket.on('interactive', ...)` anon at `server.ts:1777` (39 → target ≤ 30)

Today: handles Block Kit button interactions (`perm:allow:<id>` / `perm:deny:<id>` / `perm:more:<id>`). Big branch on `verb` + access.allowFrom gate + pendingPermissions lookup + approval aggregation + message update.

**Proposed extraction:**
- `handlePermissionAction(body, match): Promise<void>` — move the entire body after `await ack()` into a named function. The anon becomes a 5-line wrapper.
- Further split `handlePermissionAction` into `handleMoreAction` / `handleAllowAction` / `handleDenyAction` if the extracted function is still over 30. Profile before splitting further — a single extraction may be enough.

**Risk: MEDIUM-HIGH.** This is the permission-approval surface. NIST two-person integrity tests (policy.ts + server.test.ts end-to-end) must stay green.

### 4. `mcp.setRequestHandler(CallToolRequestSchema, ...)` anon at `server.ts:850` (84 → target ≤ 30)

Today: the master `switch(name)` for every MCP tool. Currently dispatches at least 6 tools (reply, upload, set_chunk_policy, set_chunk_mode, list_sessions, publish_manifest based on prior inspection) — each `case` is itself ~30-50 lines.

**Proposed extraction (larger surgery):**
- Lift each `case 'X': { ... }` body into its own `executeX(args, ctx): Promise<MCPResult>` function. The anon becomes a dispatch table: `const handler = handlers[name]; return handler ? handler(args, ctx) : unknownTool(name)`.
- Each `executeX` individually should land under 30.
- Optionally: move the handlers to their own file (`tools.ts`) to keep `server.ts` focused on Slack + MCP wiring.

**Risk: MEDIUM.** Largest LOC change but most mechanical — each `case` is already self-contained. The Zod input validation at the top of the anon stays in place.

## Acceptance criteria

- `bun scripts/crap-score.ts --threshold 30` exits 0 (no function above 30)
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` step updated to `--threshold 30` (tightened from 85)
- `bun run typecheck` clean
- `bun test --timeout 15000` — all existing tests pass bit-for-bit (669 as of main; refactor may not change the count)
- `features/steps/*.ts` scenarios all pass against the refactored primitives
- `bash scripts/coverage-floor.sh 95` — coverage does not drop below the existing 98.43% / 98.75%
- Stryker run on lib.ts (ccsc-y4e's tests) still reports ≥ 84% mutation score — no lost kills from the gate() refactor
- `bunx depcruise --config .dependency-cruiser.js .` — 0 violations (31-A.4 etc. still enforced)
- `bash scripts/harness-hash.sh --verify` — OK (no .feature files touched)
- CHANGELOG.md entry under Unreleased / Changed

## Out of scope (explicit)

- Adopting Biome (`ccsc-dz8`) — separate bd
- Wiring Stryker in CI (`ccsc-0mn`) — separate bd
- Moving handlers to `tools.ts` — can be bundled IF the complexity win is large enough, but strictly the bd only requires bringing all four under 30. File-splitting is an additional judgment call.

## Suggested sequencing

1. Start with `server.ts:850` (the 84-complexity MCP dispatch) — largest gap, most mechanical, lowest per-branch risk.
2. Then `server.ts:1777` (interactive handler) — medium complexity, single responsibility.
3. Then `handleMessage` — small extraction of the `deliver` branch.
4. Finish with `gate()` — smallest gap but highest security risk; do it last when you have the most surrounding coverage confidence.
5. Tighten CI threshold to 30 as the final commit of the PR.

Each function refactor can be its own commit on one branch; the CI-threshold flip is the closing commit.

## References

- `scripts/crap-score.ts` — the measurement tool (PR #135 / ccsc-gh0)
- `000-docs/QUALITY_GATES.md` §8c — the Wall 5 gate row
- `000-docs/MUTATION_REPORT.md` — Stryker baseline that must be preserved
- `features/inbound_gate.feature` + `features/steps/gate.ts` — Wall 1 scenarios against `gate()`
- `server.test.ts` — unit + integration coverage (669 tests at time of bd)
- `~/.claude/skills/audit-tests/references/crap-and-complexity.md` — the skill's Wall 5 rubric

## Risk posture

**gate() is security-critical.** Any diff that touches it should:
- Ship with sub-agent architecture review (code-reviewer or architect-reviewer)
- Keep every test green bit-for-bit — no "I'll fix that test to match the new behavior" moves
- Re-run Stryker post-refactor and confirm ≥ 84% kept on lib.ts
- Not change the public API shape of `GateResult` or `GateOptions` — those are contracts
design: Strategy per function: (1) gate() at lib.ts:1113 → extract handleBotEvent() + handleDmEvent() as pure helpers; gate() becomes a thin 5-line router. (2) handleMessage at server.ts:2066 → extract deliverEvent() for the case 'deliver' body. (3) socket.on('interactive') anon at server.ts:1777 → extract handlePermissionAction() past the ack() call; further split into per-verb handlers if needed. (4) CallToolRequestSchema anon at server.ts:850 → lift each switch case into executeX() handlers; anon becomes a dispatch-table lookup. Sequencing: tackle largest gap first (server.ts:850 at 84), finish with highest-risk (gate() at 32).

title: Review and triage GitHub code-scanning alerts
description: Periodic sweep of https://github.com/jeremylongshore/claude-code-slack-channel/security/code-scanning. Known open: CodeQL alert #20 (js/file-system-race false positive on server.test.ts realpath+statSync in tmpdir test; already resolved as a PR thread, but the security-tab alert needs UI dismissal with 'used in tests' rationale). Walk the full list, dismiss false positives with rationale, file beads for real ones.
notes:
Triage complete 2026-04-19 (end of v0.7.0 session). All three currently open
alerts are non-actionable; attach these notes to the UI dismissal.

---

### Alert #19 — ERROR · DangerousWorkflowID · .github/workflows/gemini-review.yml:46
**Dismiss reason:** won't fix

> Accepted risk with documented mitigations. The `pull_request_target` + head-SHA
> checkout pattern is intentional so fork PRs receive AI review (see CHANGELOG
> v0.4.0, #34). Mitigations in place: (1) `persist-credentials: false` — no
> write token available to PR code; (2) checkout by SHA not ref — blocks
> force-push TOCTOU; (3) only action executed is `run-gemini-cli`, which is a
> read-only AI reviewer with restricted shell tools; (4) workflow is read-only
> by design. The GitHub SecurityLab post this rule cites addresses the classic
> "pwn request" pattern where PR code gets a write token or can execute
> arbitrary build steps — neither applies here.

### Alert #20 — warning · js/file-system-race · server.test.ts:3157
**Dismiss reason:** used in tests

> Test fixture, not production code. The flagged pattern is `statSync(p)` →
> `readFileSync(p)` inside a unit test that just created the file via
> `saveSession()` moments earlier. No concurrent writer exists in the test
> harness between the stat (mode check) and read (content check), so there is
> no real TOCTOU window. Flagging this would require either inlining a single
> `readFileSync` + mode-from-stat call (harms test clarity) or adding
> file-descriptor plumbing to the test, both of which add complexity for no
> security gain in a test-only context.

### Alert #21 — warning · js/file-system-race · journal.ts:414
**Dismiss reason:** won't fix

> Out of threat model. The flagged line is `fsOpen(opts.path, 'a', 0o600)` in
> JournalWriter initialization. CodeQL fires because the earlier reverse-chunk
> read (to recover lastHash and nextSeq from the existing audit log) is
> followed by this open-for-append, creating a stat-then-use window. A real
> exploit would require an attacker with write access to
> `~/.claude/channels/slack/` (mode 0o700, single-writer by design). An
> attacker inside that directory already has write access to `.env` (tokens),
> `access.json` (allowlist), and `sessions/*` — swapping the audit log with a
> symlink is strictly less powerful than what they already possess. Per
> THREAT-MODEL.md, write access to the state directory is outside the attack
> surface we defend against. Bead ccsc-otd tracks restructuring this open path
> to do the hash-chain read via a single file handle, which would incidentally
> close this CodeQL path.

---

**Action tomorrow:** UI dismiss all three with the reasons/comments above,
then close this bead. API dismissal was attempted and blocked by sandbox
(scope: "comment" ≠ "dismiss") — this is intentional friction, not a bug.

title: Build ccsc audit-key {init, rotate} operator CLI
description:

- New CLI entry point (maybe scripts/audit-key.ts or a server.ts --audit-key-init flag): 'ccsc audit-key init' generates a fresh Ed25519 keypair via generateKeyPair(), writes audit.key.sops.yaml.tmp via serializeKeyPairYaml, sops-encrypts in place (subprocess), atomic rename to audit.key.sops.yaml. - 'ccsc audit-key rotate --reason=<scheduled-90day|compromise-suspected|operator-initiated>': loads current keypair, generates new keypair, opens audit.log, writes one final system.key_rotation event under the OLD key (input.old_public_key + input.new_public_key + input.rotation_reason), atomic swap of audit.key.sops.yaml (old → audit.key.sops.yaml.<timestamp>.archived). Prints the new public key for the operator to update gist + pass.

- Refuse to operate if SLACK_TMUX_SESSION or admin-commands wired (operator must STOP the bridge before key rotation).

- Round-trip via parseKeyPairYaml matches what generateKeyPair produced

title: !mute <agent> operator verb — human-initiated loop break for peer bots
description:
When two peer bots get stuck in a loop in a channel (despite the rate-limit), a human in the channel should be able to type '!mute @CodexBot' and the inbound gate drops CodexBot's messages from that channel for a TTL (default 5 min). After TTL, mute auto-clears.

Rides on the admin-command machinery being built in ccsc-3w0 (admin.ts dispatcher, virtual policy tools, audit events). !mute is a new admin verb that:
- Requires the issuer to be on the channel's allowFrom list (same rule as !clear / !restart)
- Does NOT require HMAC nonce + cross-channel confirmation (ccsc-ofn) — !mute is non-destructive and reversible, so the cost/benefit of nonce friction doesn't apply
- Takes a Slack @mention as argument; resolves to bot_id; stores (channel, bot_id) → expiresAt in an in-memory mute store
- gate() consults the mute store on every inbound peer-bot message; if (channel, bot_id) is muted and not expired, drops with reason 'admin.muted'
- New EventKind: admin.mute
- Counterpart: !unmute <agent> for early release before TTL

title: Per-bot per-channel rate limit to break A→B→A runaway loops
description:
When two peer bots are opted into the same channel via allowBotIds, A's reply triggers B which triggers A which triggers B — infinite loop unless something breaks it. The existing global rate limit + event-dedup TTL helps but doesn't specifically target the cross-bot case.

Concrete shape: extend the per-channel state in lib.ts to track (channel, sender_bot_id) → message count over a rolling window. If any (channel, sender_bot_id) pair exceeds a threshold (e.g., 10 msgs in 60s), the inbound gate starts dropping that bot's messages from that channel until the window expires, and the system journals a gate.inbound.drop event with reason 'rate.cross_bot_loop'.

This is purely defensive — humans can still post freely. The cap only applies to allowlisted PEER BOTS. Existing rate limits stay in place.

Acceptance:
- New per-(channel, bot_id) sliding-window counter in lib.ts (likely 60s window, 10 msg threshold — operator-tunable)
- gate() drops over-limit peer-bot messages with reason 'rate.cross_bot_loop'
- Journal records the drop with bot_id + channel
- Per-bot threshold operator-configurable via ChannelPolicy.peerBotRateLimit
- ~15 unit tests covering boundary conditions, threshold reset on window expiry, per-bot independence (one bot exceeding doesn't affect another)

title: Multi-agent Slack channels — humans + multiple AI agents converse together
description:
Capability epic. CCSC's four-principal model + Epic 31 manifest protocol already make multi-agent channels architecturally possible. What's missing is the operator-facing experience: how to set it up, how to prevent runaway loops between bots, and how to break a stuck exchange.

End-user scenario:
- Channel #design-review has Jeremy + Claude (his agent) + CodexBot + GeminiBot
- Jeremy: '@Claude check the test suite; @CodexBot do the same on your side'
- Claude: 'Tests passing 835/835. Coverage 97.04% line.'
- CodexBot: 'Tests passing 412/412. Coverage 94%.'
- Jeremy: '@Claude draft a PR that bumps CodexBot's coverage'
- Claude: 'On it. Reading CodexBot's project...'

Already shipped:
- allowBotIds per-channel opt-in (Epic 31-A, T3 mitigation)
- requireMention per-channel — mention-driven addressing
- Self-echo filter — bot doesn't reply to its own messages
- read_peer_manifests MCP tool (Epic 31-A) — bot can see peer capabilities
- publish_manifest MCP tool (Epic 31-B / ccsc-0qk) — bot advertises its own capabilities
- Hash-chained tamper-evident audit + Ed25519 signing (ccsc-22l) — every cross-agent message recorded
- Manifest invariant: 'advertisements are not grants' (Miller 2006) — peer claims don't bypass policy

Missing pieces for the operator experience (filed as child beads):
1. Per-bot per-channel rate limit — prevents A→B→A runaway loops (global rate limit doesn't catch the cross-bot case)
2. !mute <agent> operator verb — human-initiated loop break (rides on ccsc-3w0 admin command machinery)
3. Multi-agent setup recipe doc — operator walkthrough: 'I have two bots, how do I make them play together in one channel'
4. (Optional) slack/announce_task MCP tool — structured Block Kit messages agents can use to coordinate without duplicating work

Scope guardrails (explicit non-goals):
- E2E encryption — Slack workspace admins see plaintext; out of scope (different trust boundary; that's an Envoy-shape problem, not a CCSC-shape problem)
- Cross-workspace federation — Slack Connect handles this; CCSC doesn't need new code
- Agent-runtime ownership — CCSC stays a bridge; each agent runs its own runtime (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, whatever). CCSC governs the chat surface, not the agent execution.

Sequencing: this epic lands AFTER the current rollout (#167) closes. The HMAC nonce + admin commands work in the rollout's tail provides the foundation for the !mute verb. Don't start until ccsc-3w0 is merged.

title: Extend detectShadowing for cross-tier intersection (not just subset) detection
description:

title: HMAC nonce + cross-channel confirmation flow for destructive admin verbs
description:
Prerequisite to ccsc-3w0 (admin commands). The EchoLeak threat class (CVE-2025-32711) and the 'Your AI, My Shell' result (84% attack success) make pure same-channel verb matching unsafe for destructive admin operations. Industry consensus (OpenAI Agents SDK HITL, Microsoft Agent Framework, n8n HITL) is cross-channel confirmation with single-use server-minted nonces.

Adds:
- lib.ts exports: mintNonce(secret, ttlMs) → { nonce: string; expiresAt: number }, verifyNonce(nonce, secret, store) → boolean (single-use enforcement via in-memory store)
- server.ts: when admin command requires confirmation, mint nonce, send as Slack DM to requesting user via chat.postMessage with channel=user_id
- admin.ts: parse <nonce> token from follow-up command, call verifyNonce, refuse on miss/expiry/replay

Schema: none — in-memory state only; nonce store doesn't persist (intentional — restart invalidates pending nonces, which is the conservative posture).

Tests: ~12 new tests covering mint/verify happy path, single-use enforcement, TTL expiry, wrong-channel reject, replay reject.

title: Add tiered rule priorities (Default / Workspace / User / Admin) to policy.ts
description:
Pattern stolen from Gemini CLI's TOML rule tiers + Codex CLI's Starlark execpolicy strictest-wins resolution.

CCSC's policy.ts currently has detectShadowing for catching rule ambiguity but no explicit tier model — all rules implicitly live at one level. As soon as CCSC supports more than one operator per channel (or per-tenant deployment), the lack of tiering forces every override into shadowing-detection territory.

Concrete shape: extend PolicyRule Zod schema with tier: 'default' | 'workspace' | 'user' | 'admin' (default = 'workspace' for backward compat). Resolution: final_priority = tier_base + (rule_priority/1000). Strictest-tier-wins, with 'admin' tier reserved for ops/security overrides that per-channel users cannot override.

References:
- Gemini CLI: docs/reference/policy-engine.md — Default=1 / Extension=2 / Workspace=3 / User=4 / Admin=5
- Codex CLI execpolicy: codex-rs/execpolicy/README.md — Starlark prefix_rule() with allow/prompt/forbidden, strictest-wins

Cost: ~1 epic. Benefit: makes CCSC deployable in cohort / multi-operator contexts (e.g., Anthropic Enterprise Program cohort, Intent Solutions partner engagements) without inventing a new auth model. Provenance: 2026-05-17 harness comparison pass.

Captures asymmetric override: admin auto_approve beats workspace deny (intended Admin-overrides path); admin deny beats workspace auto_approve (the silent-footgun ccsc-4g8 lints for). title: Strip denied tool-call attempts from agent context window
description:
Pattern stolen from Gemini CLI (google-gemini/gemini-cli, docs/reference/policy-engine.md). When CCSC's policy.evaluate() returns a deny decision, the agent's context window still contains the attempted call — which can encourage the model to retry or work around the denial in subsequent turns. Gemini CLI's policy engine explicitly excises denied calls from the next prompt, achieving a stronger information-flow boundary.

Concrete shape: extend the deny path in policy.ts to mark events as 'memory-excise' and have the dispatcher rewrite the next agent-bound prompt to omit the attempted call's trace. Coordinate with journal.ts (the journal still records the attempt; the agent just doesn't see it on subsequent turns).

Cost: low — ~1 epic. Benefit: defends against model-side retry loops that can amplify operator-coercion attacks. Provenance: 2026-05-17 harness comparison pass; citation https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/blob/main/docs/reference/policy-engine.md

Minimal MCP notification carrying ONLY { request_id, behavior: 'deny' } — no rule id, no reason, no input echo. Closes the retry-rephrase loop. Two helpers extracted into new policy-dispatch.ts module (mirrors acp-adapter.ts pattern — pure functions testable without server.ts boot-time side effects): buildDenyNotificationParams pins wire-format invariant (type alias rather than interface per Gemini round-1 — eliminates index signature loophole, locks the wire shape to exactly 2 fields at compile time); recordPolicyDenyToJournal enforces order-of-operations contract with audit-resilience (second write attempted even when first throws). New EventKind policy.deny.context_stripped. § Context-stripping on policy.deny added to 000-docs/policy-evaluation-flow.md documenting what CCSC can excise (the MCP notification response) vs cannot (Claude Code's KV cache) and why response minimisation is the implementable floor for an MCP-bridge architecture. title: Stream Claude Code output to Slack incrementally via chat.update
description:
Empirically the strongest single intervention for perceived-latency in chat-driven LLM systems. Practitioner consensus across OpenAI (developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latency-optimization), Anthropic Claude TTFT benchmarks, and Redis blog (redis.io/blog/streaming-llm-responses): streaming first token within ~600ms collapses the perceived-latency problem.

Beats any thinking-indicator UI affordance (Gnewuch et al. 2022 BISE — typing indicators are neutral-to-irritating for experienced users like Jeremy). NN/g threshold model implies streaming makes the 1s/10s thresholds moot.

Scope: hook into MCP server's tool-result stream (or Claude's stream_event NDJSON if reachable), buffer to a stable chunk size, emit chat.postMessage for the initial chunk, chat.update for subsequent. Need to keep audit-projection (Epic 30-B) coherent — each update is still one logical event, not N events. Rate-limit awareness: Slack chat.update is 1 req/sec per channel.

Provenance: 000-docs/research-admin-commands-2026-05-17.md §Open follow-up questions #3.

New stream-reply.ts sibling module ships streamReply(opts, deps) — progressive Slack reply via chat.update on a cached ts. New EventKind system.stream_finalize. Locked design contract: exactly TWO journal events per stream (one gate.outbound.allow at start carrying pre-committed full-text SHA-256 + expected_chunks; one system.stream_finalize at end carrying chunks_sent + matching committed_hash). Per-chunk assertOutboundAllowed runs on EVERY chunk (no per-chunk events but defensive gate check happens every time) — channel removal mid-stream → finalize with deny + reason → failed_mid_stream result. title: Upgrade journal.ts to Ed25519-signed Merkle checkpoints
description:
Currently journal.ts is hash-chained only (SHA-256 prevHash/hash per event). 

The 2026-05-17 harness comparison pass surfaced that Hermes-Agent's own cryptographic-audit-trail proposal (NousResearch/hermes-agent#487) was CLOSED WITHOUT SHIPPING in-tree — the thread converged on a stronger conclusion that hash chains alone are insufficient against an operator with write access, and that the proper shape is Ed25519-signed receipts + RFC 8785 JCS canonicalization + policy_attestation with policy_digest (SHA-256 of the canonical policy doc) inside the signed payload.

Three independent reference implementations have shipped this shape with CI-checked cross-implementation interop test vectors:
- Signet (Prismer-AI/signet) — Rust
- nobulex (arian-gogani/nobulex) — Node.js  
- AgentLedger (dembovvski/agentledger) — Python

LangChain RFC #35691 specifies the policy_attestation core profile (referenced in Hermes #487 thread).

Concrete shape for CCSC: extend each journal.ts event to include policy_attestation: { policy_digest: 'sha256:<hex>', policy_decision: 'permit'|'deny' } where policy_digest is the SHA-256 of the JCS-canonicalized current policy.ts rule set; then sign the entire event (including hash, prevHash, and policy_attestation) with an Ed25519 key. Optionally publish head signature to an external trust anchor (Sigstore Rekor, public git tag) — but even without that, signed receipts + policy_digest are strictly better than bare hash chain.

This puts CCSC ahead of Hermes (which intended to ship this but didn't), AEGIS (Yuan et al. 2026), and Right to History (Zhang 2026).

Provenance: 000-docs/research-admin-commands-2026-05-17.md and the 2026-05-17 harness comparison pass. Citations: github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent/issues/487 ; github.com/Prismer-AI/signet ; github.com/arian-gogani/nobulex ; github.com/dembovvski/agentledger.

JournalWriter accepts signingKey + policyDigest options, emits v2 signed events when key present, v1 otherwise (backward-compatible). verifyJournal walks mixed v1/v2 chains, rejects v2->v1 rollback as tamper, switches active public key on system.key_rotation events (RFC 6962 CT pattern), validates signatures under currently-active key. policyDigest() in policy.ts computes SHA-256 of canonicalized sorted-by-id rules — opaque hex string crosses module boundary, enforced by new no-journal-imports-policy depcruise rule. Two Gemini medium-priority suggestions applied (YAML trailing-comment stripping, derivePublicKey SPKI prefix check). 828 tests pass (787 → 828, +41). Coverage 98.21% line / 99.32% func. title: Design pairing.accepted journaling: file-watcher vs IPC vs server-side pairing
description: Split off from ccsc-rc1. pairing.accepted is emitted when a user runs /slack-channel:access pair <code> — but the skill runs in Claude Code's process, not the MCP server. Server only sees access.json mutations on next getAccess() load, which is too late and lossy (multiple acceptances could collapse into one load). Three design options, each with tradeoffs: (1) File-watcher: server.ts uses fs.watch/chokidar on access.json, diffs prev vs. new state, journals pending→allowFrom transitions as pairing.accepted. Pro: no skill changes. Con: racy (missed events during server downtime), diff-based inference not authoritative. title: Evaluate capability-token formats (macaroon / biscuit / UCAN / DPoP-bound JWT) for delegated operator control
description:
Premature until a second principal (e.g., supervisor-bot, ops-rotation operator, peer-bot delegated admin) is in flight, but worth a tracking bd so the design doesn't get reinvented under deadline.

Current state: operator identity = Slack user ID in access.allowFrom. Strata 2026 survey: 93% of agent projects still use unscoped API keys; the corrective is short-lived per-action proofs. The 2025-2026 capability-token formats:
- Macaroon (Fly.io operational implementation since 2024; HMAC-chained caveats; offline attenuation)
- Biscuit (Eclipse Foundation 2024; Ed25519 chained sigs + Datalog policy; AIP cites it as chained-mode primitive)
- UCAN (DID-based public-key chain; trustless local-first)
- DPoP-bound scoped JWT (SuperTokens, Strata recommend for AI agents)

Pragmatic floor for now: per-action HMAC nonce (server-minted challenge, operator echoes in reply) — ~30 LoC, prevents replay and chat-history-poisoning attacks. Full macaroon/biscuit overbuilt until multi-operator delegation is a real requirement.
